description: Palms flat, elbows straight, lean in gently and read the angle. Your wrist extension decides whether push-ups, planks, and handstands are medicine or poison for you. Here is the ninety-degree line, why wrist tendons grumble, and the graded loading that earns the range back.

lines: all of them pay this toll.
beats.title: EVERY PUSH COSTS WRIST

scenes.narration: Put both palms flat on a table, fingers pointing back toward your body, elbows straight but soft. Now lean your shoulders forward gently, travelling over your hands, until you feel the wrists reach their honest limit: a strong stretch, the first whisper of pain, or palms that want to lift at the heel of the hand. Stop there and look at the angle between your forearm and the back of your hand. A fully open wrist approaches ninety degrees, forearm upright over a flat palm. Most adults are nowhere near it, and they find out the hard way, mid push-up, when the wrist files its complaint at full bodyweight. That angle, plus any pain number you felt, is your Wrist Pain Test. Remember both. At the end of this video I will grade them, and show you how wrist tendons actually heal.

lines: Range without pain is the goal.
beats.title: ANGLE AND PAIN, BOTH

scenes.label: A FULLY OPEN, QUIET WRIST
scenes.narration: Here is the line. NINETY degrees of extension with a flat palm and no complaint is a wrist that can pay the toll for any pushing exercise you will ever do. Between sixty and ninety, you own the common pattern: enough range for daily life, not enough for floor work at full load, which is why push-ups hurt people who are otherwise fine. Pain arriving before sixty degrees, or pain that is sharp rather than stretchy, means the wrist's tendons and joints are irritated, and load needs to be rebuilt, not endured. Notice the test grades two things at once: the ANGLE and the PAIN. Chasing angle while ignoring pain is how wrists get worse. Respecting pain while never visiting range is how they stay stiff. Healing is the two numbers walking toward each other.
scenes.sub: 90 deg quiet: full toll - 60-90: floor-work gap - pain before 60: irritated

beats.text: EVERY FINGER HAS A CABLE HERE

scenes.narration: Look at what your wrist actually is. Eight small bones in two rows form a bridge between forearm and hand, and across that bridge runs the entire traffic of the hand: the tendons that curl your fingers, the tendons that open them, nerves, and blood vessels, all threaded through tight tunnels of tissue. There is no spare room in this design. When tendons get irritated and slightly swollen, the tunnel gets crowded, and crowded tunnels complain exactly the way yours does: stiffness in the morning, pain under load, a wrist that feels older than the rest of you. Extension, the position from your test, is where the tunnel tightens most, which is why the floor is such an honest examiner. The wrist is not weak. It is busy, crowded, and honest about its limits. Healing means calming the traffic and widening the road, in that order.

beats.title: TWO WAYS BACK TO THE FLOOR

lines: the angle while you rebuild it.
beats.title: THE WORKAROUND IS LEGIT

scenes.narration: The road back has a strict order, and skipping steps is why wrists stay angry for years. First, calm the irritation: a short period of lighter load, positions that do not provoke it, and gentle movement that keeps the tunnels gliding. Then, graded loading: isometrics for the wrist muscles, then controlled range, then partial weight on the palm at easy angles, a wall before a counter, a counter before the floor. Notice the legitimate workaround hiding in plain sight. While you rebuild, push-ups on FISTS or on handles keep the wrist straight and let you train everything else at full effort. That is not cheating. That is dosing. The flat palm is a position you earn back on the tendon's schedule, and the schedule is measured in weeks of quiet, progressive work, not in toughness.

beats.text: USE IT OR LOSE THE ANGLE

scenes.narration: Step back and look at the modern wrist's day. It types with the hands hovering in slight flexion, scrolls with the thumb doing overtime, drives, texts, and then, twice a week, is asked to slam into ninety degrees of extension under bodyweight and perform. The failure is scheduled by the lifestyle. Tissue keeps the ranges it visits and quietly surrenders the ones it does not, and extension is the least-visited range in modern life. The fix is partly environmental: keyboard height that lets the wrist float neutral, phone breaks for the thumb, and small daily visits to the extended position at tolerable loads, a few seconds on the desk, a few on the wall. You are not only rehabilitating a joint. You are renegotiating its daily contract, one ordinary hour at a time.

Your advantage is, once again, the dose. Weight-bearing wrist work loads the joint with a fraction of your bodyweight, and your fraction is the smallest in the room. A heavy man's first wall press is a serious event for an irritated wrist; yours is a gentle conversation. That means you can visit the healing zone daily, adjust the angle by centimetres of lean, and progress in steps fine enough that the tissue never has to shout. Wrist rehab punishes the powerful and rewards the precise, because the structures are small and their tolerance bands are narrow. Your whole build is a precision instrument for exactly this kind of work. The guys who muscle through wrist pain are not tougher than you. They are just working with a blunter tool.
Now load it with me. Palm on the table, press down gentle and steady, no movement, no pain spike. Thirty seconds each side, fifteen to rest, three rounds. Go.

beats.text: PAIN AFTER A FALL = GET SEEN

scenes.narration: Your week runs in the right order. Isometric presses daily at a comfortable effort, gentle range visits several times a day, and weight-bearing that climbs the staircase: wall this week, counter when the wall is boring, floor when the counter is quiet. The mistakes that keep wrists loud: grinding full push-ups through pain because the program says so, which re-irritates the tunnels faster than they can calm. Aggressive stretching into the painful end range. And the opposite sin, wrapping the wrist up and using it for nothing, which guarantees a weaker, stiffer joint. The honest line: wrist pain that began with a fall on an outstretched hand, pain with swelling, clicking with weakness, numbness in the fingers, or pain that simply never improves, see a professional if it persists. Wrists hide fractures and ligament injuries well. They deserve a proper look when the story is wrong.

scenes.label: THEN WE LEAN IN AGAIN
scenes.narration: So, your grade. Pain before sixty degrees means calm it first: two weeks of isometrics and easy range before any serious palm loading, and fists for your pushing work meanwhile. Sixty to ninety, quiet but short, is the floor-work gap, the most common grade here: graded angles will close it, and your push-ups move to a counter until they do. Ninety degrees and quiet means the toll is paid in full; train the floor like you own it, because mechanically, you do. Watch the two numbers walk toward each other over the month, angle rising, pain falling. That is tendon-and-joint healing you can measure with a table. Put your angle in the comments. Just the number. We lean in again in thirty days.
scenes.sub: pain before 60: irritated - 60-90: floor-work gap - 90 quiet: full toll

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same table, same gentle lean, and we grade that wrist again. Subscribe, because next we open the mistake files: the five errors quietly destroying tendons all over your body. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
